prompt_free_text:
This paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a modification of Transformer self-attention that augments autoregressive language models with an explicit stack-like latent state derived from incremental constituency parsing. The core idea is to maintain a “stack tape” of token depths under a shift-reduce style incremental parse, supervise attachment decisions from silver or gold parses, and use the resulting depth values to additively bias attention logits. Empirically, the paper reports gains on Dyck generalization, BLIMP and SG syntactic evaluation, improved sample efficiency on a parsed Wikipedia corpus, and modest downstream gains when fine-tuning GPT-2 with Pushdown Layers.

Overall, I found the paper interesting, technically nontrivial, and well motivated. The work addresses a real weakness of standard self-attention—its lack of explicit recursive state—and proposes a mechanism that is more lightweight than prior syntax-aware generative models that linearize parse actions into the token stream. The paper’s strongest contribution is conceptual: it shows a plausible middle ground between unconstrained Transformers and heavily structured transition-based syntactic LMs. The empirical results on syntactic generalization are also quite compelling, especially the gains over a standard LM without sacrificing perplexity, and the sample-efficiency results on WikiTrees are suggestive that the inductive bias is useful beyond small controlled settings.

That said, I also have several concerns about the framing, the fairness and completeness of the empirical comparisons, and some unresolved questions about scalability, inference, and what exactly is being learned. My overall assessment is positive, but I think the paper would be stronger with clearer ablations and a more careful discussion of what benefits come from explicit recursive bias versus simply injecting supervised parse-derived features.

The method is elegant. The stack tape representation is simple enough to be implemented in parallel during training, which is a major practical advantage over transition-sequence syntactic LMs. The use of depth embeddings as additive key offsets is also appealing because it preserves the standard attention machinery and allows the model to learn how strongly to use the structural signal rather than hard-coding attention masks. This “soft structural bias” is a meaningful design choice and, in my view, one of the paper’s main strengths. The attachment mechanism is also intuitive: the model predicts the next token and an attachment point in parallel, then updates the stack tape synchronously. This gives the model a joint distribution over strings and parses without expanding the output vocabulary to include structural actions.

The empirical section is broad and generally convincing on the narrow claim that Pushdown Layers improve syntactic generalization under supervised parse annotations. The Dyck experiments are a good sanity check and show the intended recursive bias clearly. The BLLIP/BLIMP/SG results are the most important, and here the gains over the base Transformer are substantial. It is particularly notable that the model improves SG suite performance from 69.5 to 82.3 while keeping perplexity essentially unchanged. That is a strong result because it suggests the model is not merely trading off language modeling quality for syntactic competence. The comparison to PLM and TG is also useful, especially since Pushdown Layers avoid tripling sequence length with structural tokens.

I also appreciated the attempt to test larger-scale relevance via WikiTrees and GPT-2 fine-tuning. Many syntax-aware LM papers stop at sentence-level PTB/BLLIP settings, so it is good to see an effort to move toward more realistic corpora and pretrained models. The sample-efficiency claim on WikiTrees is one of the more practically interesting findings in the paper.

However, several aspects of the evaluation leave room for doubt.

First, the method relies on supervised constituency parses, often silver parses from an external parser. This is not a minor implementation detail; it is central to the approach. The paper is generally honest about this, but some of the framing occasionally overstates the generality of the contribution. The model is not simply learning recursion from language modeling pressure; it is being trained with explicit structural supervision and then using that supervision at inference through predicted attachments. Therefore, comparisons to plain LMs are informative about the value of supervised syntax, but less informative about whether the architectural change itself is the key ingredient. A stronger empirical decomposition is needed.

In particular, I would have liked to see ablations that separate: replacing attention with Pushdown Layers but removing attachment supervision; keeping attachment supervision but not using the stack tape to modulate attention; using gold or silver depth features as side information without the autoregressive attachment model; and varying how many layers are replaced. The paper includes a base LM with an attachment loss in the Dyck setting, which is good, but analogous ablations on natural language are missing. Without them, it is hard to know whether the gains come from the specific pushdown computation, from multi-task syntactic supervision, or simply from injecting parse-derived depth embeddings into attention.

Second, the comparisons to prior structured models are not entirely clean. The paper emphasizes that Pushdown Layers do not add structural tokens and therefore avoid the computational overhead of PLM/TG-style models. That is a fair advantage. But the perplexity comparisons are partly non-comparable due to tokenization differences, and BLIMP for TG is missing. More importantly, the inference procedures differ substantially. Pushdown-LM uses approximate marginalization with beam search over parses, and SG surprisal is computed from beam states at each time step. This is reasonable, but it introduces another axis of complexity and approximation. Since beam size is fixed at 300, I would like to know how sensitive the reported gains are to beam size, and whether the base LM or competing structured models are evaluated under equally optimized inference settings. The paper argues that it avoids word-synchronous decoding, but beam search over latent parses is still a significant inference burden.

Third, the scalability story is mixed. The paper claims the FLOPs are similar to standard attention but acknowledges a substantial memory increase due to 3D key tensors. This is not a small caveat. In modern Transformer training, memory bandwidth and activation storage are often the bottlenecks. The asymptotic memory increase from storing per-query per-source depth-conditioned keys could be quite serious for long contexts. The paper would benefit from concrete wall-clock and memory benchmarks, especially for the WikiTrees and GPT-2 experiments. “Drop-in replacement” is somewhat overstated if the memory overhead materially limits context length or batch size in practice.

Fourth, the parsing analysis is interesting but somewhat awkwardly interpreted. The model is trained on parser-produced silver trees and then evaluated against PTB and BLLIP trees, with binarization and filtering of unknown-word sentences. Achieving high unlabeled F1 is impressive, but it is not obvious what this demonstrates beyond the fact that the model can imitate the structural supervision it received. Since the training annotations on WikiTrees and perhaps BLLIP are themselves parser-derived, the parsing result is less a test of emergent structure than of supervised structural modeling. I do not think this invalidates the result, but the paper should be more cautious in presenting it as evidence of broad parsing ability.

Fifth, the downstream GLUE gains are modest and somewhat underdeveloped. Improvements of 0.3–1 point on a few tasks are nice, but the setup is fairly elaborate: first fine-tune GPT-2 medium as an LM on parsed WikiTrees with Pushdown Layers, then parse each downstream dataset, precompute stack tapes, and fine-tune for classification via prompting. This pipeline depends on external parsing and task-specific preprocessing, and the gains are small enough that it is hard to judge practical significance. I would not treat this as a major contribution unless accompanied by stronger evidence, significance testing, or a broader task suite.

There are also some conceptual questions about the representation itself. The stack tape stores token depths, not full constituent identities or labels. This is attractive for simplicity, but it also means the model only gets a compressed structural signal. It would be useful to understand what information is lost relative to richer tree encodings, and whether depth alone is sufficient for the reported gains. Relatedly, the attachment decision is made to the rightmost token of a constituent. This induces a particular canonicalization of incremental parses. The paper says the parse is built as a unique sequence of stack-tape updates, but I would like a clearer argument that this representation is expressive enough for arbitrary binarized constituency trees and that the induced action sequence is indeed unique under the chosen convention.

Another issue is robustness to parser noise. Since WikiTrees is automatically parsed, and the method depends directly on those parses, one would expect some sensitivity to annotation quality. The paper would be much stronger with an experiment varying parse quality or injecting noise into the stack tape supervision. This is especially important because one of the main practical use cases is large-scale silver data.

I also think the paper could do more to situate itself relative to simpler syntax-feature baselines. For example, what if one simply adds supervised depth embeddings or constituent-boundary embeddings to token representations, without the explicit stack update mechanism? Or uses parse-distance biases in attention, akin to relative position biases but tree-derived? The current comparisons are mostly against either plain Transformers or much heavier structured generative models. That leaves open whether Pushdown Layers are the right level of complexity.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper makes a meaningful contribution. The idea is novel, the method is reasonably well specified, and the main syntactic generalization results are strong. The work is especially valuable because it proposes a structured inductive bias that is neither fully hard-constrained nor purely latent, and because it integrates with autoregressive Transformers in a relatively natural way. I can imagine this line of work being influential for future research on explicit memory mechanisms in attention models.

For improvement, I would most strongly recommend the following. First, add ablations isolating the effects of structural supervision, attachment prediction, and attention modulation. Second, report practical training/inference costs, including memory, throughput, and beam-search sensitivity. Third, compare against simpler syntax-informed attention biases or feature-injection baselines. Fourth, clarify the uniqueness and expressivity of the stack-tape representation and discuss failure modes under noisy parses. Fifth, tone down claims around “drop-in replacement” and downstream generality unless supported by stronger efficiency and transfer evidence.

In summary, this is a strong and creative paper with convincing evidence on syntactic generalization, but with some important caveats about supervision, efficiency, and attribution of gains. I lean positive because the core idea is novel and the main results are substantial, though I would expect a camera-ready version to address the ablation and efficiency gaps more thoroughly.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a replacement for standard self-attention that augments Transformer language models with an explicit stack-like memory represented as a stack tape of token depths in an incremental constituency parse. The model jointly predicts next tokens and attachment decisions, uses supervised parses to precompute stack-tape states during training, and injects depth embeddings into attention keys to softly bias attention toward recursive structure. Empirically, the method improves generalization on Dyck languages, BLIMP, and SG syntactic test suites, appears more sample-efficient on a parsed Wikipedia corpus, and yields modest gains on several GLUE tasks after staged fine-tuning of GPT-2.
strengths: Clear and novel architectural idea: introducing an explicit stack-inspired state into Transformer attention while preserving the standard token output space.
The method is conceptually appealing as a soft structural bias rather than a hard attention mask, and is presented as a drop-in replacement for self-attention.
Strong empirical gains on syntactic generalization benchmarks, especially SG suites and Dyck extrapolation, relative to a standard Transformer baseline.
The paper compares against relevant structured baselines such as PLM, PLM-Mask, and Transformer Grammars, and the reported results are competitive or better on several syntactic evaluations.
The sample-efficiency results on WikiTrees are interesting and support the claim that explicit structural supervision can improve syntactic generalization under limited data.
The analysis section provides some interpretability evidence via parsing quality and attention behavior on agreement tasks.
The paper is generally well motivated and connects the proposal to prior work on recursive structure, syntactic language modeling, and memory-augmented neural networks.
weaknesses: The approach depends on supervised constituency parses, often silver parses, which substantially limits generality and makes improvements partly attributable to external syntactic supervision rather than the architectural bias alone.

The claim that Pushdown Layers are a drop-in replacement is somewhat overstated: training requires parse annotations and inference requires beam search over latent parses to approximate sentence probabilities.

The empirical comparisons are not always fully controlled. Some baseline perplexities are not directly comparable due to tokenization differences, and structured baselines rely on numbers taken from prior work.
The GLUE improvements are small and limited in scope, with gains on only 3 of 4 tasks and no evidence on larger or more diverse downstream benchmarks.
The memory overhead is substantial due to 3D key tensors, weakening the practical appeal despite similar FLOP counts.
The paper does not sufficiently disentangle how much of the gain comes from the auxiliary attachment supervision versus the specific stack-tape attention modulation.
The method is restricted to unlabeled binarized constituency structure and English-centric experiments, leaving unclear how robust it is across languages or parsing formalisms.
methodological_flaws: There is a mismatch between training and inference: during training the model conditions on precomputed gold stack tapes and gold attachments, whereas at inference it uses its own predicted attachments. This exposure-bias-like discrepancy is central to the method but is not carefully analyzed.

The probabilistic formulation in Eq. (7) defines a joint model over words and parses, but most reported syntactic evaluations rely on approximate beam marginalization with a fixed beam size of 300. The sensitivity of conclusions to beam size and search errors is not reported, which weakens empirical validity for BLIMP/SG comparisons based on p(x).

The attachment mechanism uses argmax decisions to update the stack tape during inference, making the latent structural process effectively deterministic given beam state. The paper does not justify whether this search procedure is adequate for approximating the intended probabilistic model or whether alternative parses with similar probability materially affect results.

The claim in Section 3.4 that Pushdown Layers have the same number of operations as standard self-attention is incomplete/misleading from a practical methodology standpoint: the construction introduces O(n_d n_s d) memory for key tensors and likely nontrivial indexing/batching overhead, so computational comparability is not established empirically with runtime benchmarks.

The parsing evaluation is not fully fair: the model is trained on parser-produced silver trees and then compared against the same parser on BLLIP-derived data, and on PTB the evaluation excludes sentences with unknown words. This makes the parsing-quality evidence less convincing as an independent validation.

The paper lacks stronger ablations. In particular, there is no clear comparison among: (i) attachment supervision only, (ii) depth embeddings only, (iii) varying number/location of Pushdown Layers, and (iv) alternative structural features. Without these, the causal contribution of the proposed mechanism is not fully established.

Some broad claims about recursion being fundamentally challenging for self-attention are stronger than what the presented evidence supports, since the experiments focus on specific syntactic benchmarks and supervised structural settings rather than a comprehensive test of recursive computation.
